events.title: Hertz Proves EM Waves
events.description: Heinrich Hertz proves the existence of electromagnetic waves, the foundation of radio.

events.title: Marconi's First Experiments
events.description: Guglielmo Marconi begins his first wireless telegraphy experiments in Italy.

events.title: Term 'Radio' Coined
events.description: The term 'radio' is coined by French physicist Édouard Branly.

events.title: First Amateur Experiments
events.description: The first 'amateur' wireless experiments are reported in hobbyist magazines.

events.title: First Transatlantic Signal
events.description: Marconi sends the first transatlantic wireless signal (the letter 'S') from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

events.title: Hertzian Wave Instructions
events.description: Amateur Work magazine publishes instructions on building a 'Hertzian wave' system for hobbyists.

events.title: International Telegraph Conference
events.description: The first International Telegraph Conference in London discusses the need for wireless regulation.

events.title: Invention of the Diode
events.description: John Ambrose Fleming invents the thermionic valve (diode), a key radio component.

events.title: UK Wireless Telegraphy Act
events.description: The UK passes the Wireless Telegraphy Act, the first law requiring radio licenses.

events.title: First UK Licenses Issued
events.description: The first UK 'Experimental' licenses are issued to 68 pioneering individuals.

events.title: Invention of the Triode
events.description: Lee de Forest invents the Audion (triode), enabling electronic signal amplification.

events.title: First Voice Transmission
events.description: Reginald Fessenden makes the first wireless voice and music transmission on Christmas Eve.

events.title: First US College Radio Club
events.description: The Wireless Telegraph Club of Columbia University is formed, the first US college club.

events.title: Radio Club of America Founded
events.description: The Junior Wireless Club (later Radio Club of America) is founded in New York.

events.title: First Radio Call Book
events.description: The first 'Call Book' listing radio stations is published by Modern Electrics magazine.

events.title: World's First National Society
events.description: The Wireless Institute of Australia (WIA) is founded, the world's first national radio society.

events.title: Sinking of the Titanic
events.description: The Titanic disaster highlights the critical need for 24-hour radio watches and regulation.

events.title: US Radio Act of 1912
events.description: Following the Titanic, the US passes the Radio Act, relegating amateurs to '200 meters and down'.

events.title: Amateur First Grade Licenses
events.description: The US Department of Commerce begins issuing the first official 'Amateur First Grade' licenses.

events.title: Q-Code Adopted
events.description: The 'Q-Code' is internationally adopted to standardize radio shorthand communication.

events.title: RSGB Founded
events.description: The Radio Society of Great Britain (RSGB) is founded to represent British amateurs.

events.title: Regenerative Circuit Developed
events.description: Edwin Armstrong develops the regenerative receiver circuit, vastly improving sensitivity.

events.title: Founding of the ARRL
events.description: Hiram Percy Maxim and Clarence Tuska found the American Radio Relay League (ARRL).

events.title: First Issue of QST
events.description: The ARRL publishes the first issue of QST magazine, the journal for radio amateurs.

events.title: WWI Dismantle Order
events.description: The US enters WWI; all amateur stations are ordered to dismantle and store their equipment.

events.title: Superheterodyne Receiver
events.description: Edwin Armstrong develops the superheterodyne receiver while serving in the military in France.

events.title: ARRL Defeats Navy Monopoly
events.description: The US Navy attempts to maintain a monopoly on radio; the ARRL successfully lobbies Congress against it.

events.title: Amateurs Return to Air
events.description: US amateurs are allowed back on the air on October 1st following the post-WWI ban.

events.title: Transatlantic Tests Fail
events.description: The first ARRL Transatlantic Tests fail to hear US amateur signals in the United Kingdom.

events.title: Godley Hears US Hams
events.description: Paul Godley (1BCG) travels to Scotland and successfully hears dozens of US hams, proving shortwave propagation.

events.title: Official Call Signs Assigned
events.description: The US government begins assigning official call signs, replacing self-chosen initials.

events.title: First 2-Way Transatlantic Contact
events.description: Leon Deloy (8AB) and Fred Schnell (1MO) achieve the first two-way amateur contact across the Atlantic.

events.title: Amateur Extra License Created
events.description: The 'Amateur Extra First Grade' license is created in the US for top-tier operators.

events.title: Shortwave Discovery
events.description: Amateurs discover that 'short waves' (below 100m) allow for reliable global daytime communication.

events.title: Formation of the IARU
events.description: The International Amateur Radio Union is founded in Paris to coordinate global amateur activity.

events.title: Worked All Continents (WAC)
events.description: The Worked All Continents (WAC) award is established to recognize global communication.

events.title: Washington Conference Allocations
events.description: The Washington Conference officially allocates the 80, 40, 20, and 10-meter bands to amateurs.

events.title: Federal Radio Commission (FRC)
events.description: The Federal Radio Commission (FRC) is created in the US to regulate the growing radio spectrum.

events.title: Amateur First Class License
events.description: The 'Amateur First Class' license grade is introduced in the United States.

events.title: Early SSB Experiments
events.description: Robert Moore (W6DEI) begins early experimental Single Sideband (SSB) voice transmissions.

events.title: Creation of the FCC
events.description: The US Communications Act of 1934 creates the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

events.title: License Classes A, B, and C
events.description: The FCC implements the Class A, B, and C amateur license structure.

events.title: DXCC Rules Drafted
events.description: The first rules for the DX Century Club (DXCC) are drafted to reward contacts with 100 countries.

events.title: Hiram Percy Maxim Passes
events.description: ARRL founder Hiram Percy Maxim passes away; W1AW is established as his memorial station.

events.title: DXCC Award Launched
events.description: The DXCC award is officially launched, becoming the premier award in amateur radio.

events.title: Cairo Conference Loss
events.description: The Cairo Conference results in amateurs losing parts of the 40-meter band to international broadcasters.

events.title: WWII Shutdown
events.description: US amateurs are ordered off the air following the attack on Pearl Harbor.

events.title: WERS Created
events.description: The War Emergency Radio Service (WERS) is created to allow hams to assist in civil defense.

events.title: Bands Reopen Post-War
events.description: Amateur bands begin to reopen after WWII; the 10-meter band is the first to return.

events.title: 2-Meter Band Allocated
events.description: The 2-meter band (144 MHz) is allocated to amateurs, replacing the old 2.5-meter band.

events.title: 15-Meter Band Created
events.description: The Atlantic City Conference creates the 15-meter band (21 MHz) for amateur use.

events.title: Invention of the Transistor
events.description: The transistor is invented at Bell Labs, paving the way for compact, solid-state radio gear.

events.title: SSB Superiority Demonstrated
events.description: Oswald Villard (W6QYT) demonstrates that SSB is superior to traditional AM for amateur voice.

events.title: Novice and Technician Classes
events.description: The FCC introduces the Novice and Technician license classes to encourage new hams.

events.title: 40m Phone Band Opens
events.description: The 40-meter band is opened to voice (Phone) communication for the first time in the US.

events.title: RTTY Authorized
events.description: The first Radio Teletype (RTTY) authorizations are granted to US amateur operators.

events.title: Novice License Popularity
events.description: The Novice license becomes a major entry point for the 'Space Age' generation of hams.

events.title: First Transatlantic SSB Contact
events.description: The first two-way amateur contact across the Atlantic using Single Sideband occurs.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Tracking
events.description: Hams worldwide track Sputnik 1's beacons, providing the first public tracking data of a satellite.

events.title: Explorer 1 Tracking
events.description: Amateur operators track the first US satellite, Explorer 1, on its 108 MHz signal.

events.title: First Moonbounce (EME)
events.description: The first two-way Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) contact occurs on 1296 MHz.

events.title: OSCAR 1 Launch
events.description: OSCAR 1, the first amateur satellite, is launched and transmits 'HI' in Morse code.

events.title: US Hams Pass 250,000
events.description: The number of licensed amateur radio operators in the United States exceeds 250,000.

events.title: Incentive Licensing
events.description: The FCC introduces Incentive Licensing, tying spectrum privileges to higher-grade licenses.

events.title: OSCAR 3 Transponder
events.description: OSCAR 3 is launched, featuring the first active communications transponder on an amateur satellite.

events.title: SSTV Popularized
events.description: Slow Scan Television (SSTV) standards are popularized, allowing hams to send images over HF.

events.title: Satellite Transponder Contact
events.description: The first amateur contact via a relaying satellite transponder (OSCAR 5) takes place.

events.title: AMSAT Founded
events.description: The Radio Amateur Satellite Corporation (AMSAT) is founded to coordinate amateur space projects.

events.title: VHF FM Repeater Boom
events.description: VHF FM repeaters begin to proliferate, revolutionizing local and mobile communication.

events.title: OSCAR 6 Long-Life Satellite
events.description: OSCAR 6 is launched, the first long-lived amateur communications satellite in orbit.

events.title: OSCAR 7 Launch
events.description: OSCAR 7 is launched; it would famously 'come back to life' decades after its battery failed.

events.title: Solid-State QRP Boom
events.description: The 'West Coast Handbook' and new transistors popularize solid-state low-power (QRP) construction.

events.title: Vanity Call Signs Begin
events.description: The FCC begins issuing 'Vanity' call signs, allowing hams to request specific identifiers.

events.title: PCs Enter the Shack
events.description: The first personal computers (Apple II, TRS-80) begin to be used for logging and digital modes.

events.title: Russian RS Satellites
events.description: The first Soviet amateur satellites (RS-1 and RS-2) are successfully launched into orbit.

events.title: WARC-79 New Bands
events.description: WARC-79 allocates three new 'WARC bands' at 30m (10 MHz), 17m (18 MHz), and 12m (24 MHz).

events.title: First Packet Experiments
events.description: The first amateur Packet Radio experiments are conducted in Vancouver, Canada.

events.title: AX.25 Protocol Standard
events.description: The AX.25 protocol is adopted as the worldwide standard for amateur packet radio.

events.title: First Ham in Space
events.description: Owen Garriott (W5LFL) operates the first amateur station from the Space Shuttle Columbia.

events.title: Volunteer Examiner Program
events.description: The VE program begins in the US, allowing hams to administer license exams themselves.

events.title: AMTOR Error Correction
events.description: AMTOR (Amateur Teleprinting Over Radio) introduces robust error-correcting digital modes.

events.title: Early Digital Voice
events.description: The first experimental 'Digital Voice' transmissions are conducted on the HF bands.

events.title: Novice Enhancement
events.description: The FCC 'Novice Enhancement' grants voice privileges on 10m and 220MHz to entry-level hams.

events.title: OSCAR 13 Launch
events.description: OSCAR 13 is launched, providing high-altitude elliptical orbit communications for years.

events.title: No-Code Technician License
events.description: The 'No-Code Technician' license is introduced in the US, leading to a massive boom in hams.

events.title: Contact with Mir Station
events.description: The first amateur radio contact between Earth and the Mir Space Station takes place.

events.title: First SDR Concepts
events.description: The first 'Software Defined Radio' (SDR) concepts are published in amateur technical journals.

events.title: APRS Protocol Standardized
events.description: The Automatic Packet Reporting System (APRS) protocol is standardized for position reporting.

events.title: Introduction of PSK31
events.description: Peter Martinez (G3PLX) introduces PSK31, revolutionizing weak-signal digital text chat.

events.title: Sound Card Digital Modes
events.description: The first 'Sound Card' digital modes allow hams to use regular PCs instead of external modems.

events.title: License Structure Simplified
events.description: The FCC simplifies the US license structure to Technician, General, and Extra classes.

events.title: ARISS Program Begins
events.description: The ARISS program begins, facilitating school contacts with the International Space Station.

events.title: Morse Requirement Optional
events.description: The WRC-03 conference allows countries to eliminate Morse code as a licensing requirement.

events.title: D-STAR Introduced
events.description: D-STAR (Digital Smart Technologies for Amateur Radio) is introduced as a digital voice standard.

events.title: Morse Requirement Removed
events.description: The FCC officially removes the Morse code requirement for all US amateur license classes.

events.title: WSJT-X Released
events.description: Joe Taylor (K1JT) releases WSJT-X, introducing the JT65 and JT9 weak-signal digital modes.

events.title: ARRL 100th Anniversary
events.description: The American Radio Relay League (ARRL) celebrates its 100th anniversary since founding.

events.title: Release of FT8
events.description: The FT8 digital mode is released, quickly becoming the most popular mode in amateur history.

events.title: QO-100 Launch
events.description: QO-100, the first geostationary amateur radio transponder, is launched over Africa/Europe.

events.title: Record License Numbers
events.description: Amateur radio reaches a record high of over 780,000 licensed operators in the United States.
